paragraphs: The last three numbers of this series were devoted to listing the dangers to which we should be exposed, in a state of disunion, from the arms and arts of foreign nations. I shall now go on to describe dangers of a different and perhaps still more alarming kind: those that will in all probability flow from dissensions between the States themselves, and from domestic factions and convulsions. These have already in some instances been lightly anticipated, but they deserve a more particular and fuller investigation.

A man must be far gone in Utopian speculation to doubt seriously that, if these States were either wholly disunited or united only in partial confederacies, the subdivisions into which they might be thrown would have frequent and violent contests with each other. To presume a lack of motives for such contests, as an argument against their existence, would be to forget that men are ambitious, vindictive, and rapacious. To look for continued harmony among a number of independent, unconnected sovereignties in the same neighborhood would be to disregard the uniform course of human events and to defy the accumulated experience of ages.

The causes of hostility among nations are innumerable. Some have a general and almost constant effect on the collective bodies of society. Of this description are the love of power, or the desire for pre-eminence and dominion, and the jealousy of power, or the desire for equality and safety. Others have a more limited though equally active influence within their own spheres. Such are the rivalries and competitions of commerce between commercial nations. And there are others, no less numerous than either of the former, that take their origin entirely in private passions: in the attachments, enmities, interests, hopes, and fears of leading individuals in the communities to which they belong. Men of this class, whether the favorites of a king or of a people, have in too many instances abused the confidence they possessed. Taking the pretext of some public motive, they have not hesitated to sacrifice the national tranquillity to personal advantage or personal gratification.

The celebrated Pericles, to satisfy the resentment of a prostitute,(1) at the cost of much of the blood and treasure of his countrymen, attacked, defeated, and destroyed the city of the SAMMIANS. The same man was the original author of that famous and fatal war known in the Grecian annals as the PELOPONNESIAN war. He was driven either by private spite against the MEGARENSIANS,(2) another nation of Greece, or by a wish to avoid a prosecution with which he was threatened as an accomplice in a supposed theft by the sculptor Phidias,(3) or by a wish to be rid of the accusations prepared against him for wasting the funds of the state in buying popularity,(4) or by a combination of all these causes. After various turns of fortune, interruptions, and renewals, that war ended in the ruin of the Athenian commonwealth.

The ambitious cardinal who was prime minister to Henry VIII allowed his vanity to aspire to the triple crown,(5) and hoped to win that splendid prize through the influence of the Emperor Charles V. To secure the favor and support of this enterprising and powerful monarch, he rushed England into a war with France, contrary to the plainest dictates of policy and at the risk of the safety and independence both of the kingdom he governed by his counsels and of Europe in general. For if there ever was a sovereign who seemed likely to realize the project of universal monarchy, it was the Emperor Charles V, whose intrigues Wolsey was at once the instrument and the dupe of.

The influence that the bigotry of one woman,(6) the petulance of another,(7) and the cabals of a third(8) had on the policy, the ferments, and the pacifications of a considerable part of Europe in their time are topics too often discussed not to be generally known.

To multiply examples of the part played by personal considerations in producing great national events, whether foreign or domestic, according to their direction, would be an unnecessary waste of time. Those who have only a superficial acquaintance with the sources from which such examples are drawn will recall a variety of instances for themselves, and those who have a tolerable knowledge of human nature will not need such lights to form their opinion of the reality or extent of that influence. Perhaps, however, a reference that helps to illustrate the general principle may properly be made to a case that has recently happened among ourselves. If Shays had not been a DESPERATE DEBTOR, it is much to be doubted whether Massachusetts would have been plunged into a civil war.

But despite the agreeing testimony of experience on this point, there are still to be found visionary or designing men who stand ready to advocate the paradox of perpetual peace between the States, though dismembered and estranged from each other. The character of republics, they say, is peaceful. The spirit of commerce tends to soften the manners of men and to extinguish those inflammable humors that have so often kindled into wars. Commercial republics like ours, they say, will never be disposed to wear themselves out in ruinous contests with each other. They will be governed by mutual interest and will cultivate a spirit of mutual friendship and harmony.

Is it not the true interest of all nations (we may ask these projectors in politics) to cultivate the same benevolent and philosophic spirit? If this is their true interest, have they in fact pursued it? Has it not, on the contrary, invariably been found that momentary passions and immediate interest have a more active and domineering control over human conduct than general or remote considerations of policy, utility, or justice? Have republics in practice been less addicted to war than monarchies? Are not the former administered by MEN as well as the latter? Are there not aversions, preferences, rivalries, and desires for unjust acquisitions that affect nations as well as kings? Are not popular assemblies frequently subject to impulses of rage, resentment, jealousy, greed, and other irregular and violent tendencies? Is it not well known that their decisions are often governed by a few individuals in whom they place confidence, and are therefore liable to be colored by the passions and views of those individuals? Has commerce so far done anything more than change the objects of war? Is not the love of wealth as domineering and enterprising a passion as that of power or glory? Have there not been as many wars founded on commercial motives, since commerce became the prevailing system of nations, as were formerly caused by the greed for territory or dominion? Has not the spirit of commerce, in many instances, supplied new incentives to the appetite for both? Let experience, the least fallible guide of human opinions, be appealed to for an answer to these questions.

Sparta, Athens, Rome, and Carthage were all republics, and two of them, Athens and Carthage, were of the commercial kind. Yet they were as often engaged in wars, offensive and defensive, as the neighboring monarchies of the same times. Sparta was little better than a well-regulated camp, and Rome was never satisfied with carnage and conquest.

Carthage, though a commercial republic, was the aggressor in the very war that ended in her destruction. Hannibal had carried her arms into the heart of Italy and to the gates of Rome before Scipio in turn defeated him in the territories of Carthage and conquered the commonwealth.

Venice, in later times, figured more than once in wars of ambition, until, having become an object of concern to the other Italian states, Pope Julius II found means to form that formidable league,(9) which gave a deadly blow to the power and pride of this haughty republic.

The provinces of Holland, until they were overwhelmed by debts and taxes, took a leading and conspicuous part in the wars of Europe. They had furious contests with England for dominion of the sea, and were among the most persevering and most implacable opponents of Louis XIV.

In the government of Britain the representatives of the people make up one branch of the national legislature. Commerce has for ages been the predominant pursuit of that country. Few nations, nevertheless, have been more frequently engaged in war, and the wars in which that kingdom has been engaged have in numerous instances come from the people.

There have been, if I may so express it, almost as many popular wars as royal wars. The cries of the nation and the importunities of their representatives have on various occasions dragged their monarchs into war, or kept them in it, against their inclinations and sometimes against the real interests of the State. In that memorable struggle for superiority between the rival houses of AUSTRIA and BOURBON, which so long kept Europe in a flame, it is well known that the antipathies of the English against the French, seconding the ambition, or rather the greed, of a favorite leader,(10) prolonged the war beyond the limits marked out by sound policy and, for a considerable time, in opposition to the views of the court.

The wars of these last two nations have in great measure grown out of commercial considerations: the desire to supplant and the fear of being supplanted, either in particular branches of trade or in the general advantages of trade and navigation, and sometimes even the more culpable desire of sharing in the commerce of other nations without their consent.

The last war but one between Britain and Spain sprang from the attempts of British merchants to carry on an illicit trade with the Spanish Main. These unjustifiable practices on their part produced severity on the part of the Spaniards toward the subjects of Great Britain that was no more justifiable, because it exceeded the bounds of a just retaliation and was chargeable with inhumanity and cruelty. Many of the English who were taken on the Spanish coast were sent to dig in the mines of Potosi, and by the usual progress of a spirit of resentment the innocent were, after a while, confounded with the guilty in indiscriminate punishment. The complaints of the merchants kindled a violent flame throughout the nation, which soon afterward broke out in the House of Commons and was communicated from that body to the ministry. Letters of reprisal were granted, and a war ensued. In its consequences that war overthrew all the alliances that only twenty years before had been formed with sanguine expectations of the most beneficial fruits.

From this summary of what has taken place in other countries whose situations have borne the nearest resemblance to our own, what reason can we have to trust those reveries that would seduce us into expecting peace and cordiality between the members of the present confederacy in a state of separation? Have we not already seen enough of the fallacy and extravagance of those idle theories that have amused us with promises of an exemption from the imperfections, weaknesses and evils that attend society in every form? Is it not time to awake from the deceitful dream of a golden age, and to adopt as a practical maxim for the direction of our political conduct that we, like the other inhabitants of the globe, are still remote from the happy empire of perfect wisdom and perfect virtue?

Let the point of extreme depression to which our national dignity and credit have sunk, let the problems felt everywhere from a lax and ill-managed administration of government, let the revolt of a part of the State of North Carolina, the recent menacing disturbances in Pennsylvania, and the actual insurrections and rebellions in Massachusetts, declare—!

So far is the general sense of mankind from agreeing with the tenets of those who try to lull our fears of discord and hostility between the States, in the event of disunion, that long observation of the progress of society has made it a sort of axiom in politics that nearness of situation makes nations natural enemies. An intelligent writer expresses himself on this subject to this effect: "NEIGHBORING NATIONS (says he) are naturally enemies of each other unless their common weakness forces them to league in a CONFEDERATE REPUBLIC, and their constitution prevents the differences that neighborhood occasions, extinguishing that secret jealousy which disposes all states to aggrandize themselves at the expense of their neighbors."(11) This passage at the same time points out the EVIL and suggests the REMEDY.
